## Introduction

My data visualization project leverages the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) dataset to answer the question: when did computer science (CS) become such a popular undergraduate degree, and how has its popularity varied geographically and across institutions?

This question is motivated and informed by the previous data projects I have worked on as part of my job in higher education administration. Of course, the "learn-to-code" phenomenon is a ubiquitous topic in higher education. Yet, I was still surprised to see the dramatic national trend in CS degrees in the dataset.

Furthermore, as part of my previous IPEDS data project, I struggled to visualize the rich degrees granted IPEDS dataset efficiently. I wanted to maximize users' freedom to discover trends in the data across institutions. However, many visualizations used line plots, with multiple institutions shown in different colors, producing a "rainbow spaghetti" effect that obscured trends and likely discouraged exploration. Thus, for this project, I wanted to begin with a more focused question and a better understanding of effective visualization design, informed by Dr. Albers Szafir’s lectures. A toy example of the "rainbow spaghetti" problem is below (after some Python setup):

```{python}
# | label: external-modules
from datetime import datetime
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

import altair as alt
from itables import show
from vega_datasets import data
```

```{python}
# | label: local-modules
from dtsa5304.etl import get_ipeds_data, get_rainbow_spaghetti_data
from dtsa5304.util import find_project_dir
from dtsa5304.ref import fips_map, state_to_region_map
```

```{python}
# | label: rainbow-spaghetti
pasta_selection = alt.selection_point(fields=["pasta"], bind="legend")
rainbow_pasta_plot = (
    alt.Chart(get_rainbow_spaghetti_data())
    .mark_line(point=True)
    .encode(
        x=alt.X("year:Q", axis=alt.Axis(format="d"), title="Year"),
        y=alt.Y("prop:Q", axis=alt.Axis(format="%"), title="Made-up Proportion"),
        color=alt.Color(
            "pasta:N", title="Pasta Shape", scale=alt.Scale(scheme="tableau10")
        ),
        tooltip=[
            alt.Tooltip("pasta:N", title="Pasta Shape"),
            alt.Tooltip("year:Q", title="Year"),
            alt.Tooltip("prop:Q", title="Made-up Proportion", format=".2%"),
        ],
        opacity=alt.condition(pasta_selection, alt.value(1), alt.value(0.2)),
    )
    .properties(
        width=500, height=400, title="Rainbow Spaghetti - Fake Data Shown Badly"
    )
    .add_params(pasta_selection)
)

rainbow_pasta_plot.show()
```

## Data Information

IPEDS is an annual data collection project conducted by the US Department of Education that gathers information from every college that participates in federal student aid programs (virtually all institutions). To answer our question about computer science, we are more interested in the IPEDS Completions components, which tracks degrees awarded using a special taxonomy that lets us compare apples-to-apples across institutions. We will use the "Computer Science" NCSES detailed field group to ensure that we collect information on many degrees that may not be simply named "Computer Science Major."

To import these data, I leverage the excellent `scipeds` package, which utilizes a DuckDB framework. For details, please see the script `src/dtsa5304/etl.py`.

```{python}
# | label: ipeds-etl
prop_cs_df = get_ipeds_data()
```

Our basic dataset is fairly simple: for each non-profit or public institution in the IPEDS database, we have yearly counts of Bachelor's degrees and Computer Science Bachelor's degrees. The dataset is fairly large, with `{python} f"{prop_cs_df.shape[0]:,}"` rows, so I will show only the largest (by Bachelor's degrees award) institution in each state below for the latest survey year:

```{python}
# | label: state-sample
sample_prop_cs_df = (
    prop_cs_df.sort_values(
        ["state_abbreviation", "year", "bachelors_degrees"], ascending=[True, False, False]
    )
    .groupby("state_abbreviation")
    .head(1)
)
show(sample_prop_cs_df, showIndex=False)
```

Descriptive statistics for the numeric columns: 

```{python}
# | label: num-col-stats
num_col_stats_df = prop_cs_df.drop(columns="unitid").describe()
show(num_col_stats_df)
```

## Goals 

## Tasks

To visualize geographic trends in these data, we will sumarize the data at the state-year level: 

```{python}
# | label: state-year-roll-up

state_year_df = (
    prop_cs_df.groupby(["year", "state_abbreviation"])
    .agg({"cs_bachelors_degrees": "sum", "bachelors_degrees": "sum"})
    .reset_index()
)
state_year_df["prop_cs"] = (
    state_year_df["cs_bachelors_degrees"] / state_year_df["bachelors_degrees"]
)
```

Now, we have a much more managable `{python} f"{state_year_df.shape[0]:,}"` rows of data. However, viewing 50+ trendlines is still in the realm of "rainbow spaghetti." To get these data on a 2-D map, we need to arrive at a single metric for each state. 

Since our research question involves the "rise of CS", we can ask: where has the percentage of CS degree changed the most over the course of our dataset (i.e., from `{python} state_year_df["year"].min()` to `{python} state_year_df["year"].max()`). 

```{python}
# | label: prop-change
sorted_grouped_state_year_df = state_year_df.sort_values(
    by=["state_abbreviation", "year"]
).groupby("state_abbreviation")

all_time_prop_change_df = (
    sorted_grouped_state_year_df["prop_cs"].last()
    - sorted_grouped_state_year_df["prop_cs"].first()
).reset_index(name="prop_cs_change")
```

```{python}
# | label: map-setup

# Add 2-digit FIPS id column to our IPEDS data
all_time_prop_change_df["fips"] = (
    all_time_prop_change_df["state_abbreviation"].map(fips_map).astype(int)
)  # The data source below drops leading zeros

states = alt.topo_feature(data.us_10m.url, "states")

# To scale positive and negative values with a diverging palette
max_abs_change = all_time_prop_change_df["prop_cs_change"].abs().max()

click = alt.selection_point(
    name="click",
    fields=["state_abbreviation"],
    value=[{"state_abbreviation": "NJ"}],
    empty=False,
)

change_map = (
    alt.Chart(states)
    .mark_geoshape()
    .encode(
        color=alt.Color(
            "prop_cs_change:Q",
            scale=alt.Scale(
                scheme="redblue",
                domain=[-max_abs_change, max_abs_change],
                reverse=True,
            ),
            legend=alt.Legend(
                format="%",
                orient="top",
                offset=0,
                direction="horizontal",
                gradientLength=450,
                title="All Time Change in Percent of Bachelor's Degrees Awarded in CS",
                titleOrient="top",
                titleAnchor="middle",
                titleLimit=450,
            ),
        ),
        tooltip=[
            alt.Tooltip("state_abbreviation:N", title="State"),
            alt.Tooltip("prop_cs_change:Q", title="Change", format=".2%"),
        ],
    )
    .transform_lookup(
        lookup="id",
        from_=alt.LookupData(
            data=all_time_prop_change_df,
            key="fips",
            fields=["prop_cs_change", "state_abbreviation"],
        ),
    )
    .properties(
        width=500,
        height=400,
    )
    .project(
        type="albersUsa"  # Note: The territories (e.g, Guam) are dropped here, unfortunately
    )
    .add_params(click)
)
```

```{python}
# | label: state-trend-plot

line_chart = (
    alt.Chart(state_year_df)
    .mark_line(point=True)
    .encode(
        x=alt.X("year:Q", axis=alt.Axis(format="d"), title="Year"),
        y=alt.Y("prop_cs:Q", axis=alt.Axis(format="%"), title="Proportion"),
        tooltip=[
            alt.Tooltip("state_abbreviation:N", title="State"),
            alt.Tooltip("year:Q", title="Year"),
            alt.Tooltip("prop_cs:Q", title="Change", format=".2%"),
        ],
    )
    .transform_filter(click)
    .properties(
        width=500,
        height=200,
        title=alt.TitleParams(
            # Dynamic title via Vega expression
            text=alt.expr(
                "click.state_abbreviation ? click.state_abbreviation[0] + ' Trend' : 'Click Map to View Individual State Trends'"
            ),
            anchor="middle",
        ),
    )
)
```

```{python}
# | label: combined-dashboard

dashboard = change_map & line_chart
dashboard.show()
```


```{python}
# | label: regions-rollup

state_year_df = (
    prop_cs_df.groupby(["year", "state_abbreviation"])
    .agg(
        cs_bachelors_degrees=("cs_bachelors_degrees", "sum"),
        bachelors_degrees=("bachelors_degrees", "sum"),
    )
    .reset_index()
)

state_year_df["region"] = state_year_df["state_abbreviation"].map(state_to_region_map)

region_year_df = (
    state_year_df.groupby(["year", "region"])
    .agg(
        cs_bachelors_degrees=("cs_bachelors_degrees", "sum"),
        bachelors_degrees=("bachelors_degrees", "sum"),
    )
    .reset_index()
)  # Note: Territories are silently dropped here since they are not part of the census regions

region_year_df["prop_cs"] = (
    region_year_df["cs_bachelors_degrees"] / region_year_df["bachelors_degrees"]
)
```

```{python}
# | label: region-plot
region_selection = alt.selection_point(fields=["region"], bind="legend")

region_chart = (
    alt.Chart(region_year_df)
    .mark_line(point=True)
    .encode(
        x=alt.X("year:Q", axis=alt.Axis(format="d"), title="Year"),
        y=alt.Y("prop_cs:Q", axis=alt.Axis(format="%"), title="Proportion"),
        color=alt.Color("region:N", title="Region"),
        tooltip=[
            alt.Tooltip("region:N", title="Region"),
            alt.Tooltip("year:Q", title="Year"),
            alt.Tooltip("prop_cs:Q", title="Change", format=".2%"),
        ],
        opacity=alt.condition(region_selection, alt.value(1), alt.value(0.2)),
    )
    .properties(
        width=500,
        height=400,
        title="Regional CS Trend",
    )
    .add_params(region_selection)
)

region_chart.show()
```
